newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices to stay weak after mild winter - Yamani.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices to stay weak after mild winter - Yamani.

text.p: Oil prices are likely to stay depressed after a mild winter in which oil stocks showed a contra-seasonal increase, former Saudi oil minister Sheikh Ahmed Zaki Yamani said on Monday.

"Put simply there is too much oil in the market to return prices to previous levels," said Yamani in an opening address to the annual conference of the Centre for Global Energy Studies (CGES) in London.
Brent blend crude oil was trading just above $18 a barrel on Monday morning compared to an average price of $20.32 in 1996 and a peak of nearly $25 early this year.
He said stocks of oil are heading higher and there was a small global stock build in the first quarter.
Typically stocks are drawn down by more than a million barrels per day (bpd) in the first quarter as winter demand picks up.
"Because companies are extremely reluctant to boost stocks this means prompt prices will have to keep on falling to generate enough incentive...to make them hold stocks," he said.

Recently oil prices have sunk into contango with prompt prices at a discount to forward levels. But so far the price difference has not been large enough for refiners to buy extra barrels of prompt oil and keep them in tank until they are needed.
According to CGES data, the relatively mild winter in the Northern Hemisphere cut 300,000 bpd from demand in OECD countries in the first quarter of this year.
Yamani, who is chairman of CGES, noted other factors that had contributed to weaker oil prices, including Iraq. He said OPEC supply increased in the first quarter and is set to rise even further.
Saudi Arabia has, in recent years, produced above quota in the first quarter but compensated for that by producing below quota in the second quarter, he said.
"For them what matters is deliveries rather than production. We hope that this time (in the second quarter) we have a repetition of that case."
It is difficult to envisage a collective cut in OPEC partly due to difficulties opening up sectors to foreign participation, he said.
The CGES annual conference will focus on the challenges ahead for the Latin American oil industry.
Yamani projected net exports of oil from Latin America to rise to 5.5 million bpd in 2006 from 3.7 million bpd at present.
"With proven reserves amounting to 13 pct of the world total and production at only 8.5 pct, Latam oil appears under exploited," he said.
In 1996, Venezuela, Mexico and Columbia accounted for 33 pct of U.S. crude and oil product imports, up from 24 pct in 1990.
By contrast, Saudi Arabia's share fell by 2 pct to 15 pct over the same period.
